note: Second-pass CRE Set 3 items. Not copied from Set 2 or from earlier Set 3 calculations. Each display equation is on its own line.

questions.stem:
A unit follows the Weibull model in the table and has already survived 500 hours. Use \(e^{-0.75}=0.4724\), \(e^{-1}=0.3679\), and \(e^{-0.25}=0.7788\).
\[
R(t_2\mid t_1)=\frac{R(t_2)}{R(t_1)}
\]
What is the probability that it survives from 500 hours to 1,000 hours?
questions.why: Condition on the survival already observed. For this Weibull model the ratio of reliabilities is another exponential. \[ (1000/1000)^{2}-(500/1000)^{2}=0.75 \] \[ R(1000\mid 500)=\exp(-0.75)=0.4724 \] 0.3679 is the reliability of a new unit through 1,000 hours. 0.7788 is the reliability of a new unit through 500 hours. 0.5276 is the conditional unreliability. B. 0.4724

traps.A: Uses the unconditional reliability at 1,000 hours.
traps.D: Uses the unconditional reliability at the current age.

chart.title: Weibull conditional life
chart.altText: Shape beta is 2 and characteristic life eta is 1,000 hours. The unit has survived 500 hours. The question asks survival from 500 hours to 1,000 hours.

questions.stem:
A normal sample is summarized below. The critical value \(t^{*}\) is for a 95 percent two-sided interval.
\[
L=\bar x-t^{*}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
What is the lower bound, to two decimal places?
questions.why: Divide the standard deviation by the square root of the sample size before multiplying by \(t^{*}\). \[ s/\sqrt{n}=8/4=2 \] \[ L=80-2.131(2)=75.74 \] 62.95 multiplies \(t^{*}\) by \(s\) and skips \(\sqrt{n}\). 77.87 subtracts \(t^{*}\) from the mean. 78.00 subtracts \(s/\sqrt{n}\) and skips \(t^{*}\). B. 75.74

traps.A: Omits the square root of the sample size.
traps.C: Subtracts the critical value from the mean.

chart.title: Normal sample for a mean
chart.altText: The sample mean is 80, the sample standard deviation is 8, and the sample size is 16. The 95 percent critical value t star is 2.131.

questions.stem:
Five units are tested independently. Each has mission reliability 0.90.
\[
P=R^{n}
\]
What is the probability that all five survive?
questions.why: Independent survivals multiply. The result is not the reliability of one unit and not the probability of exactly one failure. \[ P=(0.90)^{5}=0.5905 \] 0.3281 is the probability of exactly one failure. 0.4095 is the probability of at least one failure. 0.9000 is one unit. C. 0.5905

traps.A: Computes the binomial probability of exactly one failure.
traps.B: Computes the probability that at least one fails.
traps.D: Reports the reliability of a single unit.

chart.title: Independent mission trial
chart.altText: Five independent units are each started on one mission. Each mission reliability is 0.90.

questions.stem:
Two machines are both required. Their steady-state availabilities are independent.
\[
A_s=A_1 A_2
\]
What is the availability of the pair?
questions.why: A series requirement multiplies the availabilities. \[ A_s=(0.99)(0.97)=0.9603 \] 0.9700 is only the lower machine. 0.9800 is the average. 0.9997 is the availability if either machine were enough. A. 0.9603

traps.B: Uses the less available machine as the pair.
traps.D: Treats the machines as a parallel pair.

chart.title: Machine availability
chart.altText: Machine 1 availability is 0.99. Machine 2 availability is 0.97. Both machines are required.

questions.stem:
An accelerated test has a known acceleration factor \(AF\) from the use condition to the test stress. The test ran for \(t_s\) hours.
\[
t_u=AF\,t_s
\]
How many equivalent hours at the use condition does the test represent?
questions.why: Multiply the test time by the acceleration factor. Do not divide. \[ t_u=5(120)=600 \] 24 hours divides 120 by 5. 120 hours ignores the acceleration. 125 hours adds the factor to the test time. D. 600 hours

traps.A: Divides the test time by the acceleration factor.
traps.C: Adds the factor to the laboratory time.

chart.title: Accelerated exposure
chart.altText: The acceleration factor from use stress to test stress is 5. The test ran for 120 hours.

questions.stem:
A Jelinski-Moranda model gives the failure intensity after \(i\) faults have been removed. \(N\) is the initial fault count and \(\phi\) is the stated per-fault intensity.
\[
\lambda=\phi(N-i)
\]
What is the intensity after two faults have been removed?
questions.why: Two removed faults leave six. The intensity uses the faults still in the software. \[ \lambda=0.03(8-2)=0.18 \] 0.03 is the per-fault intensity. 0.06 multiplies by the number removed. 0.24 uses all eight faults as if none had been removed. C. 0.18

traps.A: Reports the intensity of one fault.
traps.B: Multiplies by the number of faults removed.

chart.title: Jelinski-Moranda inputs
chart.altText: The software starts with 8 faults. Each remaining fault contributes 0.03 to the failure intensity. Two faults have been removed.

questions.stem:
Two independent units are in active parallel. Either unit can carry the function. Their mission reliabilities are \(R_1\) and \(R_2\).
\[
R=1-(1-R_1)(1-R_2)
\]
What is the mission reliability of the pair?
questions.why: The pair fails only when both units fail. \[ R=1-(1-0.80)(1-0.90)=0.98 \] 0.72 multiplies the reliabilities and requires both. 0.85 averages them. 0.90 keeps only the stronger unit. D. 0.98

traps.A: Requires both units, which is a series model.

chart.title: Active parallel pair
chart.altText: Unit 1 mission reliability is 0.80. Unit 2 mission reliability is 0.90. Either unit can carry the function, and the units are independent.

questions.stem:
Expected annual loss is frequency times consequence. Frequency is events per year.
\[
E=fc
\]
Which risk has the highest expected annual loss, and what is that loss?
questions.why: Rank by the product, not by the largest consequence or the largest frequency. \[ E_A=0.04(20000)=800 \] \[ E_B=0.20(3000)=600 \] \[ E_C=0.01(50000)=500 \] Risk C has the largest consequence and the smallest expected loss. C. Risk A, 800 dollars

traps.D: Selects the consequence instead of the expected loss.

chart.title: Annual risk comparison
chart.altText: Risk A occurs 0.04 times per year with a 20,000 dollar consequence. Risk B occurs 0.20 times per year with a 3,000 dollar consequence. Risk C occurs 0.01 times per year with a 50,000 dollar consequence.

questions.stem:
Repair time is exponential. The repair rate is \(\mu\) per hour. Use \(e^{-0.5}=0.6065\).
\[
P(T\le t)=1-e^{-\mu t}
\]
What is the probability that a repair finishes within 1 hour?
questions.why: The probability of finishing by time \(t\) is one minus the probability that the repair is still open. \[ \mu t=0.5(1)=0.5 \] \[ P(T\le 1)=1-0.6065=0.3935 \] 0.6065 is the probability that the repair is still open at 1 hour. 0.5000 treats the rate as the probability. 0.6321 is \(1-e^{-1}\), the probability of finishing within the 2-hour mean. A. 0.3935

traps.B: Uses the repair rate as a probability.
traps.C: Reports the probability that the repair exceeds 1 hour.

chart.title: Exponential repair
chart.altText: The mean repair time is 2 hours, so the repair rate is 0.5 per hour. The interval asked is 1 hour.

questions.stem:
Life-cycle cost over the stated life is the purchase price plus the expected repair cost.
\[
LCC=P+nc
\]
Which design has the lowest life-cycle cost, and what is that cost?
questions.why: The lowest purchase price is not the lowest life-cycle cost. \[ LCC_A=400+6(50)=700 \] \[ LCC_B=550+2(50)=650 \] \[ LCC_C=300+10(50)=800 \] Design B costs more to buy and less over the life. B. Design B, 650 dollars

traps.A: Adds the repair cost but does not select the minimum.
traps.D: Ignores repair cost and keeps the lowest purchase price.

chart.title: Life-cycle cost of three designs
chart.altText: Design A costs 400 dollars and is expected to need 6 repairs. Design B costs 550 dollars and is expected to need 2 repairs. Design C costs 300 dollars and is expected to need 10 repairs. Each repair costs 50 dollars.
